inline.s: They upheld the Tathagata's profound Dharma treasury, guarded the Buddha-seed and kept it from being cut off, aroused great compassion and pitied sentient beings, expounded the eloquence of kindness, bestowed the eye of Dharma, blocked the three evil destinies, and opened the gate of goodness. With the Dharma given unasked they bestowed it upon the common people, like a truly filial son who loves and reveres his parents; toward all beings they looked upon them as themselves.
[Commentary]

In what was cultivated above there are two parts: first self-benefit is explained; second, from “arousing great compassion” onward, the cultivation of benefiting others is explained. Within self-benefit, “upholding the Tathagata's profound Dharma treasury” explains the cultivation of superior understanding. The nature of the Tathagata-garbha is the Tathagata's profound Dharma treasury; once the darkness of obstruction is removed, one's own mind is clearly manifest, and so it is called upholding. “Guarding the Buddha-seed and keeping it from being cut off” explains the cultivation of excellent practice. The perfections of the Dharma-realm are the Buddha-seed; guarding them so that they are free of obstruction and giving rise to good without interval is called never cut off. In benefiting others there is first the Dharma, then a simile. In the Dharma there are four sentences. First, “arousing compassion” explains the arising of a compassionate mind. Second, from “expounding the eloquence of kindness” onward, the arising of a kind mind is explained: speaking as the kind mind arises is called expounding the eloquence of kindness; understanding born of the teaching is called bestowing the eye of Dharma. Third, “blocking the three evil destinies and opening the gate of goodness” displays the benefit of the former compassion: to block means to shut off; teaching people to avoid evil, one blocks the three evil destinies; teaching people to cultivate merit, one opens the gate of goodness. Fourth, “with the Dharma given unasked, bestowing it upon the common people” displays the benefit of the former kindness. In the simile there are two sentences: first, “like a filial son loving and revering his parents” manifests the depth of the former kindness; from “toward all beings” onward, the depth of the compassion above is displayed.
Above, what was cultivated is explained; below, what was accomplished is explained.
All roots of goodness cross over to the other shore; all obtain the Buddhas' immeasurable merits; their wisdom is holy and luminous, inconceivable.
[Commentary]

“All roots of goodness cross over to the other shore” explains what was accomplished; to cross means to reach. The other shore is nirvana, and by the causal practices one reaches it, and so the cause is accomplished. “All obtain the Buddhas'” and so on explains the accomplishment of the fruit: there are merit and wisdom. “All obtain the Buddhas' immeasurable merits” explains the attainment of the Tathagata's adornment of merit. “Their wisdom is holy and luminous, inconceivable” explains the attainment of the Tathagata's adornment of wisdom: wisdom is deep and vast, beyond the measure of the conditions of feeling, beyond what speech can gauge, and so it is called inconceivable. The above is the praise of virtues.
Bodhisattvas and great beings such as these were beyond reckoning; they came together in one assembly.
[Commentary]

“Bodhisattvas such as these beyond reckoning” is the fourth section, revealing their number. All of these were shadow-and-echo figures manifesting the Dharma, and so they all came to the assembly; their minds were one in the Dharma, and so they came at one time. The above is the second [section], the listing of the assembled followers.

From here on is the third: the Tathagata manifests a sign to stir him, and Ananda opens the request. In this the text has six [passages], gathered into three pairs. The six are: 1. the Tathagata manifests a sign to stir him; 2. Ananda asks the question. This is the first pair. 3. the Tathagata asks whether he asks for himself or on behalf of those to be taught; 4. Ananda answers truthfully that he asks for himself. This is the second pair. 5. the Tathagata praises him, commands him to listen, and permits him to speak; 6. from “he replied” onward, Ananda receives the command and shows that he rejoices to hear. This is the third pair.
At that time the World-Honored One's faculties were joyful and serene; his bearing and countenance were pure; his radiant face was majestic.
[Commentary]

In the first, “at that time” indicates the time of manifesting the sign. “World-Honored One” indicates the person who manifests the sign: the Buddha is complete in all virtues and is revered by the world, and so he is titled World-Honored One. In the Indian sound it is Louqietuoqie; this is rendered World-Honored One. “His faculties joyful” and so on explains the sign manifested. “His faculties joyful and serene” shows the mark of joy: the five faculties such as the eye alike show the mark of joy, and this is called joyful and serene. “His bearing and countenance pure” shows a joyful countenance: the countenance had no sorrow, and so it is called pure. “Radiant and majestic” again displays the joyful countenance; “face majestic” again displays the joyful mark; majestic is the appearance of loftiness and excellence. Why was the Buddha joyful? Joy has two meanings. First, he thought on the virtues of practice accomplished by Amitabha Buddha, which are worthy of celebration, and so he was joyful. Second, he thought that the time for beings to gain benefit had come, and so he gave rise to joy.
The Venerable Ananda, receiving the Buddha's holy intent, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with joined palms, and addressed the Buddha.
[Commentary]

In the second section, “the Venerable Ananda” indicates the person able to ask. “Receiving the Buddha's holy intent” reveals what the request relies upon; intent means the purport of the mind. He relied on the Tathagata's mental power as though it were laid upon him, and so he raised the request. “He rose from his seat” and so on is the expedient means of opening the request; “and addressed the Buddha” and so on is the actual utterance of the words.
In the words there are three: 1. he sets forth what he himself has seen; 2. from “indeed” onward, he reveals what he has in mind; 3. from “why” onward, he concludes by asking the purpose.

Today the World-Honored One's faculties are joyful and serene; his bearing and countenance are pure; his radiant face is majestic, like a bright mirror's purity, its reflection shining through within and without. His majestic countenance is radiant, surpassing all measure; never before have I beheld such wondrous excellence as now.
[Commentary]

In the first there is first the Dharma, next the simile, then the matching. From “never before have I beheld” onward he wonders that the present differs from the past. In the Dharma he again brings up what was manifested before. In the simile, “like a mirror's reflection within and without”: the mirror's light shines outward, and this is called the reflection without; the light of the outward shining is clearly manifest within the mirror, and this is called the reflection within. The Buddha's body is thus: the light of his outward shining, the outward display, illumines the Buddha's body, and this is called reflection within and without. The matching with the simile is clear. “Never before have I beheld such wondrous excellence as now” wonders that the present differs from the past.

Indeed, Great Sage, in my mind I say: today the World-Honored One dwells in the wondrous Dharma; today the World-Hero dwells where all Buddhas dwell; today the World-Eye dwells in the practice of the guiding teacher; today the World's Finest dwells in the supreme path; today the Heavenly Honored One practices the Tathagata's virtue. Past, future, and present, Buddha is mindful of Buddha: is the present Buddha now mindful of the Buddhas?
[Commentary]

In the second, he reveals what he has in mind. Within this, first “indeed, Great Sage, in my mind I say” proclaims his own mind in general. “Indeed” carries the sense of exclusive devotion, revealing that he is single-mindedly mindful, and so it says indeed. “So” means that it is so: it reveals that what is in his mind is truly so, and so it says indeed-so. He opens it to the Buddha to let him know, and so he says Great Sage. Declaring his own mind himself is called in my mind I say. Below he displays it separately. In this, first he is mindful of what the Buddha has obtained; from “past, future, and present” onward he is mindful of what the Buddha does. In the former there are five sentences whose marks are hidden and hard to discern; let us speak of them briefly. The first sentence is general; the remaining four are particular. In the general, first “today the World-Honored One” indicates the object of the particular mindfulness: to distinguish him from other Buddhas, he says today; in the remaining sentences today is likewise. “Dwelling in the wondrous”: the Dharma obtained by the Buddha surpasses that of others and does not exist in the world, and so it is called wondrous. The four below display it in particular. The first sentence is his own virtue; the second benefits others; the third is his own virtue; the fourth benefits others. How do the first and third, both his own virtue, differ? The former is nirvana, the latter is bodhi. How do the second and fourth, both benefiting others, differ? The former is the practice that benefits others, namely the four means of gathering; the latter is the virtue that benefits others, namely the ten powers, the four unhindered eloquence, and so on. In the first, “World-Hero” is another name of the Buddha: the Buddha is the most heroic in the world, and so he is called World-Hero. “Dwelling where the Buddha dwells”: the eternal fruit of nirvana, in which all Buddhas dwell alike. Today the World-Hero dwells where they dwell, dwells in great nirvana, and can bring forth the function of transformation; therefore he is mindful of it now. In the second sentence, “today the World-Eye” is another title of the Buddha: he can open the eyes of the people of the world and cause them to see the right path, and so he is called World-Eye. “Dwelling in the practice of the guiding teacher”: the four means of gathering and so on are the practice by which the Buddha as guiding teacher transforms people. The present Buddha dwells therein; because he dwells in this practice, he now wishes to guide people to enter the Buddha-Dharma, and therefore he is mindful of it. In the third sentence, “today the World's Finest” is another title of the Buddha: the Buddha is the finest and most excellent in the world, and so he is called the World's Finest. “Dwelling in the supreme path”: unsurpassed bodhi is the supreme path; inwardly realizing the true path is the path of bodhi. The Buddha now dwells therein; because he dwells in this path, he knows the virtues of all Buddhas, and therefore he is mindful of it now. In the fourth sentence, “today the Heavenly Honored One” is another name of the Buddha. There are five kinds of gods, as the Nirvana [Sutra] explains. First, world gods: human kings, called sons of heaven. Second, born gods: the gods of the Four Kings, up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Third, pure gods: from stream-enterer up to pratyekabuddha. Fourth, gods of meaning: the bodhisattvas, because they understand the meaning of the emptiness and quiescence of all dharmas. Fifth, the god of the supreme meaning: the Tathagata, because he understands that the Buddha-nature is not empty. The Buddha is above these five kinds of gods, and so he is called the Heavenly Honored One. “Practicing the Tathagata's virtue”: the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen exclusive dharmas, the five eyes, the six superknowledges, the four unhindered eloquence and so on are the Buddha's virtues; entering into them is called practicing. Because he enters these virtues, he is able to save beings, and therefore he is mindful of it now. The above passage is mindfulness of what the Buddha has obtained. Below he is mindful of what the Buddha does; the supreme Tathagatas are the object of that mindfulness. “Past, future, and present, Buddha is mindful of Buddha” brings up others to match this. “Is the present Buddha now mindful of the Buddhas?” surmises this mindfulness of others. “Is it?” is a word of uncertainty: measuring by principle, he does not yet dare to decide, and therefore he says it.
Why is his majestic power and radiance like this?
[Commentary]
He concludes by asking the purpose. Here the first pair ends.
Then the World-Honored One said to Ananda: What do you think, Ananda? Did the gods tell you to come and ask the Buddha, or do you ask about the majestic countenance from your own wisdom and insight?
[Commentary]
The third: the Tathagata's examination. “He said: what do you think?” is the general question; “did the gods tell you” and “from your own wisdom and insight” are the particular questions.
Ananda said to the Buddha: No gods came to tell me; I ask about this meaning from what I myself have seen.
[Commentary]
The fourth: Ananda's truthful answer. “No gods taught me” answers the Buddha's former words. “From what I myself have seen, I ask about this meaning.” Here the two pairs end.

From here on is the fifth: the Tathagata praises the question, commands him to listen, and permits him to speak. Within this, first he praises what he asked; from “Ananda, you should know that the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment” onward, he brings up the Buddha's virtues, commands him to listen, and permits him to speak.

The Buddha said: Excellent, Ananda! Your question is very apt. You have brought forth deep wisdom and true wondrous eloquence, and out of pity for beings you ask this meaning of wisdom. The Tathagata, with inexhaustible great compassion, takes pity on the three realms; therefore he arises in the world, illumines and unfolds the teaching of the Way, wishing to rescue the multitudes and bestow upon them the true benefit. Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas he is hard to meet and hard to see, like the udumbara flower that appears only from time to time. What you now ask brings abundant benefit and will awaken and transform all gods and people.
[Commentary]

In the praise, first “Excellent, Ananda, your question is very apt” is the general praise. “Excellent” simply means good; “how” is a particle. According with the capacity, according with the Dharma, according with the time is called apt. From “you have brought forth deep” onward is the particular. “You have brought forth deep wisdom” praises his wisdom in asking: the five virtues of the Buddha of which he was mindful above are called bringing forth deep wisdom. “True wondrous eloquence” praises the words of his question: his praise above of the Buddha's dwelling in the five virtues is called true wondrous eloquence; being real is called true, skill of speech is called wondrous, the words can distinguish clearly and the speech is capable and skillful, and so it is called eloquence. “Out of pity for beings, asking the meaning” praises the mind of his question; it may also be called praising the purpose of the question. Ananda above brought up the Buddha's five virtues and made his request; these five virtues take wisdom as their chief, and so it is called asking the meaning of wisdom. From “the Tathagata” onward he praises the benefit of the question. In this there are four. First, the Tathagata reveals his own compassionate mind pitying beings: the Buddha's compassion is supreme, none can add to it and none can surpass it, and so it is called compassion that none can cover. Some editions of the sutra emend it to “inexhaustible”; “none can cover” is the correct reading and need not be emended. With this great compassion he pities the three realms; to pity means to have compassion. Desire, form, and formless are the three realms. Second, from “therefore” onward the Tathagata reveals that he arises in the world for the sake of beings: “therefore he arises” asks about the purpose of his arising, and below he shows it in answer. “Illumining and unfolding the teaching of the Way, wishing to rescue the multitudes” is the teaching Dharma benefiting people. “Bestowing the true benefit” is the realized Dharma benefiting beings: the principle is true and real, and teaching people is called benefit. Third, from “immeasurable billions” onward he explains that the Buddha is hard to meet: first the Dharma, then the simile. Fourth, from “what you now ask” onward he compares with the three to make clear that the question is beneficial: “what you now ask brings abundant benefit” generally explains the benefit; “awaken and transform all” explains the benefit in particular. The above is the praise of what he asked.

Below he brings up the Buddha's virtues, commands listening, and permits speaking. Within this, first he extensively brings up the Buddha['s virtues] and recounts the praise given above; from “Ananda, listen attentively” onward he commands listening and permits speaking, telling what he has in mind. Further, the former passage extensively brings up the Buddha's virtues, showing that he himself is able to teach; the latter command to listen and permission to speak show that he himself wishes to teach. In the former passage, first the supremacy of the fruit is explained; from “why is that” onward the cause is analyzed to reveal the fruit.

Ananda, you should know that the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment: his wisdom is hard to measure; he guides and governs many; his wisdom-vision is unobstructed, and none can obstruct or cut it off. With the power of a single meal he can sustain his life for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, countless and immeasurable, and even beyond that. His faculties are joyful and serene and do not decay; his bearing and countenance do not change; his radiance and face are without alteration.
[Commentary]

In explaining the fruit, first, with regard to what Ananda had in mind above, the supremacy of the Buddha's wisdom is explained. From “with a single meal” onward, with regard to the matters Ananda saw before, such as the joy of the faculties, the supremacy of the Buddha's body is explained. In explaining the supremacy of wisdom, “the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment” generally brings up the Buddha's wisdom. “His wisdom is hard” and so on specifically displays its supremacy. “His wisdom is hard to measure” explains that the wisdom is deep: he completely realizes the profound Dharma-nature of nirvana, and so his wisdom is hard to measure; this explains the wisdom as deep. This is precisely the former “dwelling where the Buddha dwells”: the wisdom that is hard to measure; realizing the Dharma is called dwelling. “He guides and governs many” explains that the wisdom is vast; this is precisely the former “dwelling in the practice of the guiding teacher.” “His wisdom-vision is unobstructed” reveals that the wisdom is sovereign: with regard to all Dharma-gates his knowing and seeing are unobstructed; this is precisely the former “practicing the Tathagata's virtue.” “None can obstruct or cut it off” displays the supremacy of his wisdom: he is not obstructed or cut off by others; displaying this mark of supremacy is called no obstruction; this is precisely the former “dwelling in the supreme path.” Below the supremacy of the body is explained. “With the power of a single meal he can sustain his life” and so on: in terms of transformation he reveals the real. Following transformation he shows that, receiving the power of a single meal, he can dwell for many kalpas without his body decaying, showing that the Buddha's essence is constant. It may also be called revealing transformation in terms of the real: because the real is constant, following transformation he manifests receiving the power of a single meal and can dwell for many kalpas without his body decaying. In the text, first “with the power of a single meal he can sustain his life for hundreds of thousands of kalpas” reveals that his life is constant. “His faculties are joyful” and so on explains that his body is constant: “his faculties are joyful and serene and do not decay,” with regard to the joy of the faculties manifested above, explains his virtue of constancy. “His bearing and countenance do not change,” with regard to the purity of bearing and countenance manifested above, explains his constant life. “His radiance and face are without alteration,” with regard to the majestic radiance and face manifested above, explains his constant samadhi.
The above, in terms of the fruit, explains that the Buddha's body and wisdom are both supreme. Below, next, the cause is brought up to reveal what accomplishes the former fruit.
Why is that? The Tathagata's samadhi and wisdom are fully pervasive and boundless; in all dharmas he attains sovereignty.
[Commentary]

“Why is that?” is a question raised to introduce: why does the Tathagata obtain this supreme wisdom and constant body? Below he answers accordingly. “The Tathagata's samadhi and wisdom are fully pervasive and boundless” explains that what he cultivates is perfected and therefore supreme. Samadhi is calming, wisdom is insight; these two are the chief of practices, and so they are singled out, while all others follow them and are therefore concealed and not discussed. Samadhi and wisdom are brought to the ultimate, and so it is called fully; they are unobstructed and sovereign, and so it is called pervasive; they are vast and boundless, and so they are called without limit. This is precisely his practice of mental sovereignty. “In all dharmas he attains sovereignty” explains that what he has learned is sovereign and therefore supreme; this is precisely his practice of Dharma sovereignty. He skillfully enters the gates of all realms; the power of the Dharma-gates manifests everywhere, and this is called sovereignty.
From the above up to here he has extensively brought up the Buddha's virtues, recounting what was praised before.
Ananda, listen attentively; now I will teach you.
[Commentary]

He commands listening and permits speaking, and will tell what he has in mind, namely mindfulness of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life in the West. “Listen attentively” is the command; “for you” is the permission. Here the fifth ends.
He replied: Indeed. I rejoice and wish to hear.
[Commentary]
The sixth: Ananda receives the command and listens. The text is clear as can be seen.
The above concludes the introductory part.

In the main body of the teaching the text divides into three. First, his practice is explained. Second, from “Ananda, the bhiksu Dharmakara has already become a Buddha and entered extinction” onward, what he accomplished is explained. Third, from “Ananda, you should know that those beings who are born in that land dwell in the right concentration” onward, those he gathers in are explained. These three are all spoken with reference to Amitabha Buddha. “His practice” reveals the immeasurable practices and vows cultivated by that Tathagata in former times. “What he accomplished” reveals the fruit of body and land that that Tathagata now obtains. “Those he gathers in” reveals that that Tathagata now gathers in the immeasurable beings of the lands of the ten directions to go together to that land, teaching and benefiting them. These three are the great outline of the sutra.

In his practice, first many Buddhas are listed, explaining the condition for the arising of practice. From “at that time there was a king who heard the Buddha teach” onward, it reveals that Dharmakara relied on this to undertake practice.

The Buddha said to Ananda: In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas ago, the Tathagata Dipankara arose in the world; he taught and liberated immeasurable beings, causing them all to attain the Way, and then entered extinction. Next there was a Tathagata named Far Light; next named Moonlight; next named Sandalwood Fragrance; next named Good Mountain King; next named Sumeru Heavenly Crown; next named Sumeru Equal Radiance; next named Moon Hue; next named Right Mindfulness; next named Free of Stain; next named Non-attachment; next named Dragon Heaven; next named Night Light; next named Peaceful Bright Summit; next named Immovable Ground; next named Vaidurya Wondrous Flower; next named Vaidurya Golden Hue; next named Golden Treasury; next named Flame Light; next named Flame Root; next named Earth Seed; next named Moon Image; next named Sun Sound; next named Liberation Flower; next named Adornment Light; next named Ocean Enlightenment Superknowledge; next named Water Light; next named Great Fragrance; next named Free of Dust; next named Renouncing Weariness; next named Jewel Flame; next named Wondrous Summit; next named Brave Standing; next named Merit-Upholding Wisdom; next named Obscuring Sun and Moon Light; next named Sun Moon Vaidurya Light; next named Unsurpassed Vaidurya Light; next named Supreme Head; next named Bodhi Flower; next named Moon Brightness; next named Sun Light; next named Flower Hue King; next named Water Moon Light; next named Removing Delusion's Darkness; next named Crossing Over the Covering; next named Pure Faith; next named Good Abode; next named Majestic Power; next named Dharma Wisdom; next named Phoenix Sound; next named Lion's Sound; next named Dragon's Sound; next named Dwelling in the World. All these Buddhas have passed away. At that time there was next a Buddha named Lokesvararaja, the Tathagata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
[Commentary]

In the former, fifty-four Buddhas are brought up together. The first fifty-three are brought up together in one place; the last one Buddha, whom Dharmakara personally served, is brought up separately in one place. Among the first fifty-three Buddhas, “in the past, inconceivable kalpas ago” and so on reveals the time. “Dipankara arose” and so on lists them in sequence. “All these Buddhas have passed away” concludes the former and gives rise to the latter. Below he next lists the Buddha Lokesvararaja. “Lokesvara” is his particular name; “Tathagata, Worthy One” and so on are his common titles. The Buddha's virtues are immeasurable; names are bestowed according to virtues, and the names are likewise unlimited. The sutra follows one count and briefly lists ten kinds. Of the ten, the first five are the Buddha's own virtues; the last five benefit others. Of the first five, the first two form one pair: the former is the perfection of the path, the latter the ultimate of cessation. The last three form one pair: the first two are the perfection of the cause, the last the ultimate of the fruit. In the first pair, “Tathagata” reveals the perfection of his path: riding the path of reality, he came and attained perfect enlightenment, and so he is called Tathagata. “Worthy One” reveals the ultimate of his cessation: he realizes cessation in accord, and so he is called worthy; moreover, because he has realized cessation, he deserves offerings, and so he is called worthy of offerings. In the latter pair, the first two are the perfection of the cause. In this, first “perfectly enlightened” reveals the perfection of his understanding; in other sutras it is also called the right and universally knowing one. “Right” is the principle; fully illumining the principle is called universal knowledge. What is here called “equal” is that “universal”: according with principle is called equal. “Right” is again the “right” of the other sutras. What is called “enlightened” is that “knowing.” “Perfect in knowledge and conduct” reveals the perfection of his practice. “Knowledge” is the practice of realization: the realization of the Dharma is clearly manifest, and so it is called knowledge. Its divisions are three, as the Nirvana [Sutra] explains: first, the knowledge of bodhisattvas, namely the prajna-paramita; second, the knowledge of the Buddhas, namely the Buddha-eye; third, the knowledge of no-knowledge, namely the eleven emptinesses. That is not intellectual understanding, and so it is called no-knowledge; it can produce the knowledge of wisdom, and so it is again called knowledge. The first two are what realizes; the latter is what is realized. Nagarjuna also says that the Buddha possesses the three knowledges, namely the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the extinction of outflows. “Conduct” is the conduct of the teaching; as the Stages of Yoga says, calming and insight are called conduct. Nagarjuna also says that precepts, samadhi, wisdom and so on are called conduct. These two are complete, and so it is called perfect. “Well-Gone” reveals the ultimate of his fruit. “Well” means good; “gone” means departed. The Tathagata has gone well, and so he is called Well-Gone. If the Buddha's virtues are complete, where else would he go, that it should say he goes well? Though there is nowhere to go, it is not that he cannot go: like the fire at the end of a kalpa, though there is nothing to burn, it is not that it cannot burn, and so it may be said to go. Of the last five, the first four are particular and the last is general. Among the first four, “knower of the world” is the wisdom that transforms others: he well understands the world, and so he is called knower of the world. “Unsurpassed one,” “tamer of men,” and “teacher of gods and humans”: these two titles are the ability to transform others. The unsurpassed one and tamer of men can tame the minds of beings; taming himself and taming others, he is the utmost among tamers, and so he is called unsurpassed. “Man” is a particular designation for a person. This unsurpassed one can with skillful means tame beings, and so he is called tamer of men. “Teacher of gods and humans” can bestow the Dharma: he can with the right Dharma instruct gods and humans closely, and so he is called teacher of gods and humans. He transforms all six paths alike, but gods and humans benefit more, and so they are singled out. “Buddha” is his virtue of transforming others: this is rendered as awakened, awakening himself and awakening others, his awakening and practice utterly complete, and so he is called Buddha. “World-Honored One” is a general title: the Buddha is complete in all virtues and is revered by the world, and so he is titled World-Honored One.
The above explains the Buddhas as the condition for the arising of practice.

Below, Dharmakara's undertaking of practice in reliance on them is explained. Within this, first his worldly practice is explained; from “the Buddha said to Ananda, when the bhiksu Dharmakara had spoken this verse” onward, his world-transcending practice is explained. What is practiced before the [first] ground is called worldly; what is on and above the ground is world-transcending.

In worldly practice there are three in order: 1. hearing the Dharma and arousing the aspiration; 2. leaving home and cultivating the Way; 3. going to the Buddha's place, paying homage with praise, and arousing the vow.
At that time there was a king who, hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, was joyful at heart and forthwith aroused the intention for the unsurpassed, true Way.
[Commentary]

In the first, “at that time there was a king” brings up the person who practices. “Hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, joyful at heart” means his mind rejoiced on hearing the Dharma. “Forthwith arousing the intention for the Way” properly explains the arousing of the aspiration. The meaning of bodhicitta is set out at length in a separate chapter, and should be fully discussed in that place.
He abandoned his country and gave up his kingship, went forth and became a shramana, and was named Dharmakara. Of lofty ability, brave and wise, he surpassed and differed from the world.
[Commentary]

In the second section, “abandoned his country and gave up his kingship” explains what he renounced. “Went forth and became a shramana” reveals what he did; shramana is rendered as one who stills, because he stills all evils. “He was named Dharmakara” lists his name. “Of lofty ability” and so on discerns his nature and conduct. “Ability” means skill; his ability and virtue surpassed others, and so it is called lofty ability. Strength of will is called bravery; clarity of mind is called wisdom. These virtues stood out alone, and so it is called surpassing and differing from the world.
He went to where the Tathagata Lokesvararaja was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with joined palms, and praised him in verse.
[Commentary]

In the third section, first he goes to the Buddha's place; next, having arrived, he shows reverence. “Bowing the head” is reverence: humbling the honored to meet the lowly, and so it is used to express reverence. “Circumambulating to the right” is love: circling without letting go, and so it is used to express love. From “knelt” onward he praises and makes vows. “Knelt with joined palms” is the expedient means of beginning the praise. “Praised him in verse” is the sutra-master's general statement. Why does it say verse? The meaning and the words are wondrous and beautiful, and those who offer praise mostly use verses; moreover, verses are skillfully concise, and in few words can gather many meanings. The bhiksu Dharmakara wished with concise words to gather the Buddha's virtues broadly, and so he used verses.

Below the words of the verses are given. First there are seven verses praising the Buddha's virtues and explaining what he seeks; afterward thirteen verses make vows seeking Buddhahood and explaining that he is able to seek.
His radiant face is majestic,
his majestic power without bound; such blazing brilliance has no equal.
The sun, the moon, and mani gems,
their pearly radiance and flame are all concealed, like a mass of ink.
The Tathagata's countenance
surpasses the world without peer; the great voice of perfect enlightenment resounds through the ten directions.
Precepts, learning, and effort,
samadhi and wisdom; majestic virtue without peer, supremely rare.
In deep and true good mindfulness
of the Buddhas' ocean of Dharma, he plumbs the depths and exhausts the mysteries, reaching its very bottom.
Delusion, craving, and anger
the World-Honored One has forever none; the lion among men, his divine virtue is measureless.
His merit is vast,
his wisdom deep and wondrous; the majestic marks of his radiance shake the thousand worlds.
[Commentary]

Among the first seven verses, the first five and a half properly praise the Buddha's virtues; the last one and a half conclude the praise of the Buddha's virtues. In the former proper praise, the first two and a half verses praise the Buddha's bodily karma; next half a verse praises his verbal karma; the last two and a half verses praise his mental karma. In praising bodily karma, “radiant and majestic” praises the supremacy of the Buddha's light and forms one section; “face majestic” praises the supremacy of the Buddha's body and forms another section. The word majestic has been explained above. There are further seven phrases displaying “radiant and majestic.” “Majestic power without bound” is that on which the emission of light depends: because the Buddha's majestic virtue and spiritual power are boundless, he can emit light. “Such blazing brilliance” properly brings up the substance of the light. “Has no equal” displays supremacy with regard to persons: the bodily light of other people cannot match it. From “the sun, the moon, and mani” to “like a mass of ink” displays supremacy with regard to things: if these lights are compared with the Buddha's light, they are all concealed, like a mass of ink beside a conch shell. The next two phrases display “face majestic”: the Tathagata's countenance surpasses the world without peer, and so his face is majestic; peer means match. Next he praises verbal karma: the great voice of perfect enlightenment resounds through the ten directions. Below he praises mental karma. Within this, first the text of two verses praises the Buddha's virtue of practice; the last half verse praises the Buddha's virtue of severance. Practice is bodhi; severance is nirvana. In the former, the first verse praises the supremacy of the Buddha's virtue and the next verse praises the depth of the Buddha's virtue. Supremacy is the practice of the teaching; depth is the practice of realization. In the former praise of supremacy, “precepts, learning, effort, samadhi, wisdom” brings up the substance of his virtues; “majestic virtue without peer, supremely rare” displays supremacy in terms of the virtues: “majestic virtue without peer” means others cannot match him, “supremely rare” means the Buddha's virtue surpasses theirs. In the latter praise of depth, “in deep and true good mindfulness of the Buddhas' ocean of Dharma” is the expedient means of approaching realization: true means carefully true; deeply thinking and truly contemplating, he is mindful of the Buddhas' ocean of Dharma, and so he can attain realization. The nature of the Tathagata-garbha is the Buddhas' ocean of Dharma. “Plumbs the depths and exhausts the mysteries, reaching its very bottom” is the accomplishment of the practice of realization. This praises the virtue of practice. Below he praises the virtue of severance: delusion is folly, craving is greed, anger is hatred; the Buddha has severed them forever, and so his severance is supreme. The above specifically praised the virtues of the three karmas; from here below he concludes the praise. “The lion among men, his divine virtue is measureless” concludes the praise in general. “His merit is vast” and so on concludes the praise in particular. “His merit is vast” concludes the praise of the former verbal karma: the great voice of perfect enlightenment resounds through the ten directions, and so the Buddha's virtue of transforming others is vast. “His wisdom deep and wondrous” concludes the praise of the former mental karma: there were many virtues before, but he concludes specifically with wisdom because it is the chief of practices; deep concludes the former depth, wondrous concludes the former supremacy. “The majestic marks of his radiance” concludes the praise of the former body. The above concludes the praise.

From here on he makes vows seeking what was praised above. Within this, first the text of ten verses properly arouses the vow-mind; the last three verses request the Buddha to bear witness. Among the first ten verses, the first five seek the Buddha's Dharmakaya; the last five seek the Buddha's Pure Land.
May I become a Buddha,
equal to the sage Dharma King, crossing over birth and death, liberating all without exception.
Giving and taming the mind,
precepts, patience, effort, such samadhi, and unsurpassed wisdom.
I vow to attain Buddhahood,
fulfilling this vow everywhere; for all who are afraid, to bring great peace.
Even if there were Buddhas,
hundreds of thousands of millions, immeasurable great sages, countless as the Ganges' sands.
To make offerings to all
these Buddhas is not equal to seeking the Way, firm and right, never retreating.
[Commentary]

In seeking the Dharmakaya, the first verse seeks the Buddha-fruit; the next two verses seek the Buddha-cause; the last two verses compare in order to display supremacy. In seeking the fruit, “may I become a Buddha, equal to the sage Dharma King” seeks the Buddha's own virtue; “crossing over birth and death, liberating all without exception” seeks the virtue of benefiting others. In seeking the cause, the first verse and a half seek the practice of self-benefit; the last half verse seeks the practice of benefiting others. In seeking self-benefit, the first verse brings up the practices of the six perfections. “Giving and taming the mind” is the perfection of giving: cultivating giving cures stinginess, and this is called taming the mind. “Precepts” is the perfection of precepts; “patience” is the perfection of patience; “effort” is the perfection of effort; “samadhi” is the perfection of meditation; “wisdom” is the perfection of wisdom; wisdom is supreme and so it is called unsurpassed. Below, in accord with this he arouses his vow: “I vow to attain Buddhahood” is the goal toward which his practice proceeds; “fulfilling this vow everywhere” is seeking the cause and its direction. Below he seeks to benefit others; the text is clear as can be seen. The above sought the cause. From here on the two verses compare in order to display supremacy and make firm his vow-mind. “Even if there were Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of millions” brings up the jewel of the Buddha; “immeasurable great sages, countless as the Ganges' sands” brings up the jewel of the Sangha. “To make offerings to these” makes offerings to the former Sangha-jewel; “to these Buddhas” makes offerings to the former Buddha-jewel. From “is not equal to seeking” onward he compares with the vow, revealing that they do not match. To retreat means to withdraw. Though one makes offerings to many sages, it is not equal to seeking the Way oneself without retreating; therefore he again makes it firm. Such comparisons are very many in the sutra and cannot all be told. Offerings are limited, while the mind that seeks the Way has no limit.
Suppose the Ganges' sands
were Buddha-lands, again incalculable, countless lands.
His light illumines them all,
pervading all these lands; such effort and majestic power are hard to measure.
May I become a Buddha
with a land supreme, its assembly wondrous, its place of enlightenment surpassing.
My land like nirvana,
without equal or peer; I shall take pity and liberate all.
Beings born from the ten directions,
their hearts joyful and pure; once they reach my land, happy and at peace.
[Commentary]

In seeking the Pure Land, the first three and a half verses concern his own pure seeking; the last one and a half verses seek a land with which to gather others. In his own seeking, the first two verses broadly bring up many lands; next half a verse explains what he himself seeks: among all lands it is the foremost. The last verse displays the mark of being foremost. In the former broad bringing up, “suppose the Ganges' sands” and so on broadly brings up many lands; from “his light illumines” onward, with regard to those many lands he explains the marks of adornment. “His light pervades these lands” explains the Buddha-Tathagata's adornment of light; “such effort and majestic power are hard to measure” explains the Buddha-Tathagata's adornment of spiritual power. The Buddha in those lands diligently manifests transforming deeds, and this is called effort; the transforming deeds are many, and so it is called majestic power hard to measure. Here the broad bringing up ends. “May I become a Buddha with a land supreme” means that among all the lands brought up before, its marks of adornment are the foremost; the present land of Amitabha that he accomplished is this. The next verse displays the mark of being foremost: “its assembly wondrous” explains that its assembly is foremost; “its place of enlightenment surpassing” explains that its place is foremost; “my land like nirvana without equal or peer” explains that the land is foremost; it may also be called foremost in bliss. The two transcriptions ni-huan and nie-pan are originally one name, differing only in how the sound was handed down, and so the text below says that in Amitabha's land beings receive bliss comparable to nirvana. The above was his own seeking. Below there is one and a half verses seeking a land with which to gather beings. “I shall take pity and liberate all” shows that when he himself in the future accomplishes the Buddha-path he will liberate all. “Beings born from the ten directions, their hearts joyful and pure” and so on shows that those in the future born in his land will all obtain excellent benefit. “Beings born from the ten directions” means those born are many; “their hearts joyful and pure” means their aspiring minds are pure; “once they reach my land” means the benefit obtained is supreme. The above ten verses properly arouse the vow-mind.
Below there are three verses requesting the Buddha to bear witness.
May the Buddha believe and know me,
be my true witness, as I make my vow there, striving with all my strength for what I seek.
World-Honored Ones of the ten directions,
whose wisdom is unobstructed, may these Honored Ones always know the course of my mind.
Even if my body should remain
among all bitter poisons, my practice shall press on; enduring to the end, I will never regret.
[Commentary]

In this text, first there is half a verse requesting the Buddha Lokesvara to bear witness for him. Next there is half a verse again arousing the vow-mind. Next there is one verse requesting the Buddhas of the ten directions to bear witness for him. Below there is one verse again arousing the vow-mind. In the first half verse, “may it be” means “I pray”: he prays that the Buddha believe that what he seeks is not vain, revealing that in the future he will certainly obtain the fruit; therefore he requests, may the Buddha believe and know me. The Buddha's witness is not vain, and so he says, be my true witness. In the next half verse, again arousing the vow, he makes vows concerning the matters he seeks there, striving diligently to cultivate what he desires: for the Dharmakaya and the Pure Land respectively he vows, striving with all his strength there for what he seeks. In the next verse, requesting the Buddhas of the ten directions to bear witness is clear. In the last verse, again arousing the vow, he concludes with an oath binding himself, and so it says, even if my body should remain among all sufferings, I will endure to the end and never regret.
The above explains his worldly practice.
The Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Life, Scroll Two, end.

blocks.text: The Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Life, Scroll Three

inline.s: Below, the world-transcending practice is explained. Within this, first the brief treatment; from “thus having cultivated, to those Buddhas” onward, the practice is explained at length. In the brief there are three: 1. Dharmakara requests, and the Tathagata answers in return, revealing that he already knows and does not proclaim it for him; 2. Dharmakara asks again for the Tathagata to teach him; 3. Dharmakara hears the teaching and practices accordingly.

The Buddha said to Ananda: When the bhiksu Dharmakara had spoken this verse, he said to the Buddha: Indeed, World-Honored One, I have aroused the mind of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. I pray that the Buddha will extensively proclaim the Dharma for me; I shall cultivate it and gather in a Buddha-land, pure and adorned, an immeasurable wondrous land, and cause me in the world quickly to attain perfect enlightenment and uproot the root of the hardship of birth and death. The Buddha said to Ananda: Then the Buddha Lokesvararaja said to the bhiksu Dharmakara: As to the practice by which you adorn a Buddha-land, you yourself should know.
